title: Approach C (matched permutation) built and benchmarked against B2; B2 lag-bias diagnosed; generator-robustness stress test reveals a shared blind spot
notes: Follow-up to common-driver-control-20260828.json (CONFIRMED, but flagged B2's power deficit and unexplained lag bias as open items). Per Hamm's 2026-08-28 instruction: treat B2 as CONFIRMED_VALID_CONTROL but not yet primary; build Approach C as a genuinely different null (timing-conditioned matched permutation, not another realignment variant); diagnose B2's bias mechanistically; build a reduced power/calibration surface; stress-test both against structurally different generators.
=== APPROACH C: DESIGN AND CALIBRATION ===

omission/jnwb_ext/common_driver_control.py: matched_permutation_pvalue bins trials by a cross-validated matched-filter jitter estimate (same estimator validated for B2) into n_bins quantile bins, then permutes R's trial assignment ONLY WITHIN bins (reusing the validated trial_permutation/permute_labels(scheme='within_group') machinery), applied to the RAW (unaligned) P/R pair -- unlike B2, no trial is ever shifted, so C does not pay B2's realignment-estimation-noise power cost.

Exchangeability was TESTED empirically, not assumed, per Hamm's explicit instruction: at n_trials=60 (B2's validated scale), naive quantile binning does NOT achieve nominal FPR even at n_bins=10 (best observed: 12.5% FP rate, vs alpha=0.05) -- the residual within-bin jitter heterogeneity is too large at this trial count for exchangeability to hold. At n_trials=200 with n_bins=20 (~10 trials/bin) and n_trials=400 with n_bins=20-40, FPR reached 0/8 in an 8-seed calibration check -- i.e. Approach C requires substantially more trials than B2 to be valid, but IS achievable at trial counts realistic for real omission sessions (hundreds of trials per condition).
=== PAIRED raw/B2/C BENCHMARK AT n_trials=200 (both methods in their valid regime) ===

omission/scripts/dev_paired_benchmark_20260828.py, omission/artifacts/.lab/paired-common-driver-control-benchmark-20260828.json. Reduced scope (5 seeds/condition, n_perm=40) due to heavy concurrent machine load from the parallel agent sweeps -- reported as indicative, not final-precision.

Negative control: raw FP=1.00, B2 FP=0.00, C FP=0.20 (1/5 -- statistically consistent with a true 5% rate at this n; P(>=1 event in 5 draws | p=0.05)=~23%, so this single event does not distinguish miscalibration from correct calibration at this sample size).
Positive control P_to_R (coupling_strength=1.2, lag=30ms): raw TP=1.00, B2 TP=0.40, C TP=0.20 (at reduced n_perm=40, lower power resolution than the dedicated power-surface sweep below).
Positive control R_to_P (coupling_strength=1.2, lag=30ms, reverse direction): raw TP=1.00, B2 TP=0.00, C TP=0.00 -- BOTH candidate controls recovered essentially nothing in the reverse direction.

CRITICAL CAVEAT on the R_to_P result: this is NOT evidence B2/C fail on reverse coupling per se -- it is a confirmed GENERATOR DESIGN FLAW. The R_to_P coupling term rides on r_sigma (narrow, low-energy relative to the shared p_center/r_center offset confound baseline), while P_to_R's coupling term rides on p_sigma (broad, high-energy, dominating the same baseline). Sign-convention check: predicted +sign for P_to_R (confirmed, recovered +36ms vs injected +30ms) and -sign for R_to_P (NOT confirmed -- observed +69ms, matching the confound's own r_center-p_center=70ms offset, not the injected coupling at all). The R_to_P test as currently built is confounded by its own generator asymmetry and must be REBUILT (symmetric kernel energies for both coupling directions) before any real conclusion about direction-symmetry can be drawn. This is flagged as an open defect in the benchmark, not a finding about the methods.
=== POWER/CALIBRATION SURFACE: coupling_strength x true_lag (n_trials=200, both methods valid) ===

omission/scripts/dev_power_surface_coupling_lag_20260828.py, omission/artifacts/.lab/dev-power-surface-coupling-lag-20260828.json. 8 seeds/cell, n_perm=60 (reduced from the requested 150 for compute-time feasibility -- disclosed, not hidden), coupling_strength in {0.6,1.2,2.0,3.0} x true_lag_ms in {10,30,60,100}, coupling_direction=P_to_R only.

Power increases with coupling_strength for both methods, roughly monotonically. AT EVERY coupling_strength >= 1.2, Candidate C's TP rate is equal to or higher than B2's (e.g. coupling_strength=2.0: C ranges 0.375-0.875 vs B2's 0.125-0.875; coupling_strength=3.0: C reaches 1.000 at lag=60 vs B2's 0.875) -- Candidate C has the BETTER power/calibration trade-off of the two methods once both are in their valid trial-count regime, contrary to the naive expectation that a realignment-based method (B2) would out-power a permutation-based method (C).

Lag bias flips sign at true_lag=100ms for BOTH methods, identically across all 4 coupling strengths (e.g. B2 at coupling_strength=3.0: bias +0.62, +2.00, +1.75ms at lags 10/30/60, then -2.38ms at lag=100). This is a reproducible, sign-consistent pattern, not noise -- flagged as an UNRESOLVED open item, root cause not yet diagnosed (candidate causes not yet checked: LAGS_MS boundary effects, kernel-width/trial_len interaction at longer lags).
=== B2 LAG-BIAS MECHANISM: DIAGNOSED, NOT JUST OBSERVED ===
omission/scripts/dev_b2_bias_diagnosis_20260828.py + .summary.json. 6 controlled ablations, n=10 seeds each (5 for two ablations), isolate the mechanism precisely.

FINDING: the ~6ms positive bias in B2's recovered lag is caused by R's OWN two-component composition (the confound-driven r_indep bump at r_center+E_i interfering with the coupling-driven bump at p_center+E_i+lag in the SUMMED cross-correlation curve's argmax) -- NOT by realignment, matched-filter estimation noise, lag-grid discretization, or circularity. Decisive evidence: (a) removing r_indep entirely collapses the bias from +5.6ms to -0.7ms; (b) the noiseless case reproduces the SAME +6.0ms bias deterministically (SD=0), ruling out noise-driven causes; (c) noiseless+no-r_indep recovers the true lag EXACTLY (0.0ms bias, every seed) -- the clean kill shot; (d) the SAME bias magnitude (+6.0ms) is present in the RAW UNALIGNED pair before any B2 realignment is applied -- B2 neither introduces nor meaningfully corrects this bias, it is orthogonal to the confound-FPR problem B2 solves; (e) P's own shift estimates are bit-identical whether coupling is on or off, ruling out estimator circularity.

GENERALIZABLE LESSON (not a benchmark-specific artifact): a single-peak-argmax lag estimator is not robust to ANY co-occurring, confound-correlated secondary response component in R. Real SPK-LFP data plausibly has exactly this structure (multiple response components sharing trial-timing structure, e.g. an early sensory-driven LFP deflection alongside a later cognitive/motor-driven one). Before trusting a recovered lag from real data: either explicitly model/subtract known-shape interfering components, or report bias as a function of secondary-component amplitude/temporal-proximity, or prefer a multi-component fit over single-peak argmax when such structure is plausible. NOT fixed in this build -- a required design consideration for the real P4 estimator, not optional polish.
=== GENERATOR-ROBUSTNESS STRESS TEST: reveals a genuine, decisive shared blind spot ===

omission/scripts/dev_generator_robustness_20260828.py, omission/artifacts/.lab/generator-robustness-20260828.json. Reduced scope (3 seeds, n_perm=50) -- variant 3's result is unanimous across all available seeds/methods and needs no further scrutiny to trust qualitatively; variants 1-2's numbers are underpowered (n=3) and should be treated as suggestive only.

Variant 1 (skewed/asymmetric kernel instead of symmetric Gaussian): raw FP=1.00 (as expected), B2 FP=0.33 (1/3, degraded from B2's ~0% on the tuned generator -- n=3 too small to confirm a real degradation vs noise, deserves a full-scope rerun), C FP=0.00 (0/3, generalizes cleanly).

Variant 2 (partially shared jitter, R's jitter = rho*E_i + sqrt(1-rho^2)*independent noise): at rho=1.0 (fully shared, replicates the original generator) B2 FP=0.00, matching prior validation. At rho=0.3, even RAW uncontrolled trial-shuffle already shows FP=0.00 -- weakening the shared jitter also weakens the very correlation it induces, so this configuration did not actually stress-test graceful degradation as intended; needs a redesign (larger effect size or bigger n) to be informative.

Variant 3 (slow latent AR(1) state across TRIALS modulating RESPONSE AMPLITUDE instead of timing, jitter_sd_ms=0 -- i.e. a PURE amplitude confound with zero timing confound): raw FP=1.00, B2 FP=1.00 (3/3), C FP=1.00 (3/3) -- UNANIMOUS FAILURE, every seed, every method, at the permutation-test floor p=0.0196. Neither B2's per-trial realignment (estimates and removes TIMING offset only) nor C's matched-permutation (bins by TIMING covariate only) does anything to protect against a confound that lives entirely in trial-to-trial AMPLITUDE rather than timing, because neither method's nuisance estimate captures amplitude information at all. This is total failure, not a subtle degradation -- both candidate controls solve ONLY the timing-jitter confound family; an amplitude-comodulation confound (e.g. a slowly-drifting arousal/session-state variable that scales both LFP and spike response gain together) would produce an equally strong false-positive-generating mechanism that CURRENT P4 controls provide zero protection against.

DIRECT IMPLICATION: before any P4 real-data directionality claim, the confound-control strategy must also address AMPLITUDE co-modulation, not just timing jitter -- e.g. by additionally conditioning/matching on an estimated trial-level amplitude/gain covariate (coarse event-response amplitude/state, one of the six candidate matching variables Hamm's original instruction already named), not by extending the timing-based methods alone.

issues.description: Both B2 and C are validated ONLY against timing-jitter confounds. A pure amplitude co-modulation confound (zero timing jitter) defeats both completely (100% FP, 3/3 seeds, both methods).
issues.action: extend the matching/control strategy to include a trial-level amplitude/gain covariate before any P4 unlock decision is finalized. This is not optional -- Hamm's own P4 unlock criterion #5 ('stable behavior across realistic jitter/noise/trial-count regimes') is not met until this is addressed, since amplitude co-modulation is a realistic real-data confound (e.g. arousal/session state).

issues.description: The paired benchmark's R_to_P (reverse-direction) test is confounded by an energy asymmetry in synthesize_adversarial_pair's coupling-term construction (narrow r_sigma-scale coupling term vs broad p_sigma-scale baseline offset), so its near-zero recovered power for reverse coupling reflects a generator defect, not a genuine finding about direction-symmetry.
issues.action: rebuild coupling_direction='R_to_P' with energy-matched kernel widths before drawing any conclusion about whether B2/C work equally well in both directions. Not yet fixed.

issues.description: Both B2 and C show a lag-bias sign flip at true_lag_ms=100 (positive bias at 10/30/60ms, negative at 100ms), consistent across all 4 tested coupling strengths -- reproducible, not noise, but root cause not yet diagnosed.
issues.action: investigate LAGS_MS boundary truncation, kernel-width/trial_len interaction, or similar structural cause before trusting recovered lags near the upper end of the tested range.

issues.description: B2's ~6ms lag bias traces to R containing a confound-correlated SECOND response component (r_indep) that interferes with the coupling-driven peak in the summed correlation curve -- a generalizable limitation of single-peak-argmax lag estimation for any signal with multiple response components sharing trial-timing structure, which real SPK-LFP data plausibly has.
issues.action: before trusting a real-data recovered lag: model/subtract known-shape interfering components, characterize bias as a function of secondary-component amplitude, or prefer multi-component fitting over single-peak argmax. Not fixed in this build.

verification.status: Round 1 back. Claim (Approach C calibrated at n_trials>=200/n_bins=20): DISPUTED -- independent verifier's larger-sample re-check (16-26 fresh seeds, not 8) found FPR ~15-19% persists at n_trials=200, contradicting this session's original 0/8 result, which the verifier attributes to a small-sample fluke (binomial P(0/8 | true rate 15-19%) = 0.25-0.34, plausible under noise). CORRECTION: the claim 'C reaches near-nominal FPR at n_trials>=200' is WITHDRAWN pending a properly-powered (30+ seed) re-check; no n_trials threshold for Candidate C should be treated as established. Claim (amplitude co-modulation defeats raw/B2/C completely): CONFIRMED, strongly -- independently reproduced on fresh seeds (9001-9006) with the exact generator code, 6/6 unanimous for all three methods, plus a mechanism sanity check (corr(P amp, R amp)=0.676 confirms genuine shared-amplitude confound; no accidental timing jitter or direct P->R dependency in the code).
verification.round2_new_findings_not_yet_independentl: Following the amplitude-blind-spot confirmation, built two multivariate nuisance-matching upgrades to Candidate C (synthesize_general_adversarial_pair + estimate_amplitude_covariate + estimate_nuisance_vector + multivariate_matched_permutation_pvalue [cartesian-product quantile stratification on [timing,amplitude]] + caliper_matched_permutation_pvalue [restricted-swap null respecting a caliper distance in standardized nuisance space], all in common_driver_control.py). Quick checks (n=6-10 seeds, NOT yet properly powered given the just-confirmed small-sample-fluke risk): (a) the safe pre-event-baseline amplitude covariate correlates r=0.86 with the true latent gain state, estimated from P alone, never touching R; (b) naive multivariate quantile stratification (cartesian product of 4 bins/dim) makes timing-only calibration WORSE (83% FP vs 17% for 1D binning) -- likely over-fragmentation from stratifying on a dimension (amplitude) with no real confound present in that scenario; (c) caliper-based matching handles the timing-only confound well (0% FP at caliper=0.5) but does NOT fully solve the amplitude confound at caliper=0.5 (100% FP, though the individual p-values were far less extreme than every other method's floor-pinned p=0.0196 -- e.g. one direct comparison gave p=0.048, right at the boundary, under a different n_perm/seed); (d) tightening the caliper shows a genuine, monotonic improvement unique to this method: FP rate 1.0 -> 0.6 -> 0.2 as caliper goes 0.5 -> 0.25 -> 0.15 (n=10 seeds each) -- the first method tested that shows real traction against the amplitude confound, though not yet fully calibrated at any caliper tested. NONE of round 2's findings have independent verification yet -- explicitly flagged, not to be treated as confirmed.
